caveats: The companies are about 1,000 of today's largest US filers, with the 500 largest picked at each past month-end by their market value that day. Companies that failed, were bought or left the exchange are missing. Only the ones that made it are here, which lifts the returns of small, volatile, cheap and money-losing companies. That is too kind to smaller size and value, and too hard on low volatility, profitability and momentum.

Company numbers are the first-filed values with their filing dates from SEC company facts, so each month uses only what was public. Later filings are used only to settle units, splits and typos. Machine-readable filings start around 2009 to 2011, which is where the test starts.

Market value is the split-adjusted close times the share count in the newest filing. Filers report share counts in mixed units, so each count is checked against the others around it: 247 companies had counts filed in thousands or millions put right, 131 spin-offs that the price history books as splits were told apart from real splits, and 71 filings with their dollars in the wrong units were set aside. Today's count is then set against today's quote: 977 of 997 companies match, 5 that do not are left out (a price quoted per depositary share, a share class the filings do not total), and 15 have no usable count (companies with several share classes that file no total). So a few very large companies are missing.
A company that merged, spun off a business or listed its shares during a month can carry the wrong share count for a month or two, until its next filing.
Analyst revisions have no free point-in-time history. The earnings growth surprise (the latest quarter against the same quarter a year earlier) stands in for them.
Costs are a flat 10 basis points a side on the names that change each month. Borrow fees on the short side and market impact are not counted.
Every stock in a fifth gets the same weight, and nothing is balanced by industry, so a factor can be an industry bet in disguise.
